answer.rationale: Finance is forcing an 18% spend cut on a component where the incumbent has refused to reopen price this cycle. A straight renewal on incumbent terms cannot satisfy the mandate and the contract expires in 14 days without auto-renew, so renewing as-is is off the table. C4 says negotiating at renewal recovered real margin when the market was used as leverage - but that lever is gone this cycle, the incumbent already said no. C2 says switching to the low-cost vendor worked sharply on unit cost, onboarding was quick, and invoicing stayed accurate. That is the direction most likely to hit the 18% target without blowing up delivery. The counter-risk is real though: C3 shows second-sourcing eliminated a single point of failure during a shortage, and this build is already running at 94% of committed volume with no buffer. So a clean, full-volume flip to a new primary on day 71, with line already tight, would be the kind of move that turns a cost win into a delivery miss. Net I intend a guarded switch: move primary to the low-cost vendor (C2 logic) but do it as a small, time-boxed ramp that builds real dual-sourced coverage (C3 logic) rather than a same-day cutover. That keeps the 18% mandate in play, avoids pinning delivery risk to a brand-new primary at peak volume, and leaves room to renegotiate the incumbent later if leverage returns. Two memories verified because the decision hinges on them: the prior switch worked (C2) and incumbent leverage at renewal is conditional, not guaranteed (C4). C1 and C5 are deliberately not pulled - renewing or deferring is no longer viable given finance's mandate and the 14-day expiry.
